Beyond Planning: Differentiable Control-in-the-loop End-to-End Autonomous DrivingThanks: Zhidong Wang, Zirui Li, Zitong Shan, Zhiqi Mao, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Jingsong Liang, and Chen Lv are with the School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore. Zhidong Wang    Zirui Li    Zitong Shan    Zhiqi Mao    Qihang Huang Affiliation: Zhan Chen, Jingsong Liang, Han Yu, and Chen Lv
Abstract

End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved remarkable progress by planning trajectories directly from raw sensor data. Yet the step from planning to control still relies on hand-tuned tracking controllers that block the gradient path from vehicle motion back to the network. This gap stems from non-differentiable vehicle dynamics, aliased supervision from coarsely sampled expert labels, rate mismatch between high-rate control and low-rate re-planning, and vehicle model discrepancies between training and deployment. This paper proposes DIVA (Differentiable Identified Vehicle dynamics for end-to-end Autonomous driving) to close this gap. An identified actuator-level vehicle model is embedded in the training loop of the end-to-end driving network, forming a differentiable chain from perception to vehicle states. A learning-based control decoder replaces the external controller and is supervised on the rolled-out vehicle states, bypassing the aliased control-input labels. A rate-consistent control-input parameterization reconciles the heterogeneous sampling rates and enables asynchronous execution with a 3.8 ms control-only cycle. On-policy re-identification and an online disturbance observer address training-time distribution shift and deployment-time model mismatch respectively. On the closed-loop Bench2Drive benchmark, DIVA achieves a driving score of 86.7, surpassing the widely adopted state-of-the-art approach by 3.3 points while nearly halving mean jerk and reducing brake switching by 64%, and maintains superior path tracking accuracy under significant vehicle model mismatch at deployment.

Index Terms: 
End-to-end autonomous driving, vehicle dynamics, system identification, differentiable simulation, motion control, imitation learning.

I Introduction

End-to-end autonomous driving unifies perception and planning within a single differentiable model that maps raw sensor data to a reference trajectory [1, 2]. Propagating the planning losses back through the perception backbone reduces the compound error that accumulates across handcrafted module boundaries. The planned trajectory serves as the imitation target and is tracked by lateral and longitudinal controllers at deployment. Training thus stops at the planning output, while closed-loop performance depends on the actual control response of the vehicle: the tracking controller, the actuator subsystems and the chassis dynamics remain outside the differentiable pipeline and block the gradient path from the vehicle response back to the network.

The execution of the end-to-end planning results relies on classical controllers designed for modular pipelines, which assume a smooth, feasible trajectory and a known vehicle model [3, 4]. An end-to-end planner satisfies neither assumption: its output is temporally inconsistent, exhibits discrete speed jumps and loses reliability over long horizons. The resulting planning-to-control discontinuity comprises three gaps. The supervision gap: expert commands are recorded at a label rate far below the control rate, yielding aliased control-input labels. The gradient gap: the non-differentiable controller and vehicle dynamics keep the training loss from reflecting the actual control response. The deployment gap: the vehicle model presumed in training differs from the deployed vehicle, and the label, perception and control rates also differ.

This paper proposes DIVA (Differentiable Identified Vehicle dynamics for end-to-end Autonomous driving) to bridge these gaps. DIVA embeds a differentiable actuator-level vehicle dynamics model in the training loop, forming a single differentiable pathway from perception to vehicle states (Fig. 1), and replaces the external controller with a learned control decoder whose supervision, gradient flow and deployment all pass through the identified vehicle dynamics model. The main contributions are:

  • •

    End-to-end autonomous driving model differentiable through to vehicle states. An actuator-level vehicle dynamics model links the planning output to the vehicle response, making the architecture differentiable from perception to vehicle states; on-policy re-identification keeps the model consistent with the learned controller.

  • •

    Dynamics-in-the-loop imitation learning in state space. Supervision on vehicle states through the dynamics model bypasses the aliased control-input labels that make direct control-input cloning ill-posed; an identifiability-aware loss and a gradient gate enable joint training of the controller and planner.

  • •

    Rate-consistent asynchronous execution at deployment. A rate-consistent control-input parameterization reconciles the label, perception and control rates; asynchronous execution decouples control from perception latency, enabling full-rate feedback and closed-loop robustness under vehicle model mismatch.

II Related Work

II-A The Planning-to-Control Interface in Autonomous Driving

In modular stacks, planning interfaces with control through a reference trajectory tracked by geometric, PID, linear-quadratic or model predictive controllers [5, 6], with modern MPC designs incorporating actuator delays and tire limits [7]. In end-to-end stacks, the output representation determines where this interface resides [8]: end-to-end networks output control commands [9], trajectory–control fusions [10], temporal trajectories [11, 12], or geometric paths to be tracked [13], where retuning controller gains alone can improve driving performance significantly [14]. Yet the training always stops at the planning output, and the learned reference trajectory is state-conditioned, temporally inconsistent and reliable only within the preview distance.

Several works extend the differentiable chain beyond the planner through kinematic or nominal vehicle models: DiffStack [15] employs a unicycle-based LQR, analytic policy gradients [16, 17] supervise through bicycle dynamics, Rodríguez-Vidal et al. [18] enable waypoint-space supervision via a kinematic model, and DIPC [19] couples a differentiable planner with a neural MPC through a six-state vehicle model with Magic Formula tires. In all cases, the vehicle model is kinematic or nominal with assumed parameters, without actuator dynamics such as slew-rate limits or lags, and the label, perception and control rates are not decoupled.

II-B Learning-based Controllers Considering Model Mismatch

Reinforcement learning [20] and imitation learning [21] can train end-to-end vehicle controllers, but the learned dynamics are implicitly encoded in the network weights and cannot be re-calibrated when the vehicle dynamics changes. The classical remedy pairs a nominal model with an observer: unknown-input observers generate steering commands [22], and adaptive Kalman filters supply tire and friction estimates to hand-designed controllers [23]. Hybrid neural–physical structures increasingly identify the nominal model itself [24, 25]. On the learning side, domain randomization tolerates a range of vehicle dynamics characters [26], and continual meta-learning adapts dynamics models online [27]. Explicit disturbance estimates have been supplied to learned quadrotor controllers [28], while for ground vehicles online adaptation refines the dynamics model within an optimizer [29]; DIPC examined certain vehicle parameter variation without retraining or adaptation [19].

These approaches remain disconnected: observer-based methods serve rule-based controllers, learned controllers absorb mismatch through domain randomization, and online adaptation refines the dynamics model rather than the controller. No existing work feeds explicit mismatch estimates to a learned controller within an end-to-end driving stack; DIVA does so by unifying model identification, differentiable planning and mismatch-aware control in a single trainable framework.

III Methodology

III-A Overall Framework

The end-to-end autonomous driving networks are supervised at the planning level; DIVA extends the differentiable computation graph to the vehicle-state level so that the training loss directly reflects closed-loop execution performance.

III-A1 Architecture Overview

Fig. 1 illustrates the overall architecture. A perception backbone fuses camera and LiDAR observations into perception tokens, from which a planning decoder produces a reference route and a target speed distribution. A subsequent control decoder maps these planning outputs together with state feedback and disturbance estimate into control-input knots that are upsampled to the control rate via first-order hold (FOH) interpolation. The identified vehicle dynamics model then propagates these control inputs forward over the prediction horizon, yielding predicted vehicle states that are supervised against the expert demonstrations. The control decoder’s outputs influence the training loss exclusively through the differentiable vehicle model: the state-loss gradient back-propagates through the vehicle dynamics into the control decoder and, modulated by a learnable gradient gate, further into the planning decoder. At deployment, the control decoder executes at every control step with cached perception features and receives an online disturbance estimate, enabling real-time mismatch-aware control.

III-A2 Problem Formulation

The planner output is a geometric path decoupled from a target speed [30], which performs markedly better in closed-loop driving than a temporal trajectory [2]. It consists of a route ℛ=(𝝆1,…,𝝆N)\mathcal{R}=(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\rho}_{N}) of NN points 𝝆i∈ℝ2\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} in the vehicle frame, uniformly spaced along the arc length, and a probability vector 𝐩v\mathbf{p}^{v} over discrete speed classes. The vehicle accepts a actuator command vector 𝐜=[ct,cb,cs]⊤\mathbf{c}=[c_{t},c_{b},c_{s}]^{\top} of throttle, brake and steering at the control rate fctrl=20f_{\mathrm{ctrl}}=20 Hz, with control period Ts=1/fctrlT_{s}=1/f_{\mathrm{ctrl}}. The expert demonstrations are recorded at flab=4f_{\mathrm{lab}}=4 Hz with label period Tlab=1/flabT_{\mathrm{lab}}=1/f_{\mathrm{lab}}: for a frame at time tt, the labels span a 2 s horizon and comprise K=8K=8 future expert states 𝐳j⋆=[Xj⋆,Yj⋆,ψj⋆,vj⋆]⊤\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{j}=[X^{\star}_{j},Y^{\star}_{j},\psi^{\star}_{j},v^{\star}_{j}]^{\top} of position, heading and speed at t+j​Tlabt+jT_{\mathrm{lab}}, j=1,…,Kj=1,\ldots,K, and the recorded expert commands, expressed as control inputs 𝐮j⋆\mathbf{u}^{\star}_{j}, j=0,…,Kj=0,\ldots,K. Perception runs at a rate fperc≤fctrlf_{\mathrm{perc}}\leq f_{\mathrm{ctrl}}, bounded by the latency of the backbone and the planner.

The control decoder 𝒞\mathcal{C} maps the memory tokens to K+1K+1 control-input knots 𝐔\mathbf{U} at the label rate. The knots are interpolated to a control-rate sequence 𝐮¯0:H−1\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{0:H-1} over H=5​KH=5K control steps, and rolled out through the identified vehicle dynamics model 𝐳k+1=ℱ⁡(𝐳k,𝐜⁡(𝐮¯k),𝜽)\mathbf{z}_{k+1}=\mathcal{F}\left(\mathbf{z}_{k},\mathbf{c}(\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{k});\boldsymbol{\theta}\right), written as 𝐳1:H=Φ(𝐳0,𝐮¯0:H−1;𝜽)\mathbf{z}_{1:H}=\Phi\left(\mathbf{z}_{0},\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{0:H-1};\boldsymbol{\theta}\right), where 𝐳\mathbf{z} is the model state and 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} collects vehicle dynamics mismatch parameters, drawn from a distribution p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) in training. The map 𝐜⁡(⋅)\mathbf{c}(\cdot) from control inputs to commands is given in Section III-B2. The control decoder is trained to solve

min𝒞⁡𝔼𝒟,𝜽∼p⁡(𝜽)​[∑j=1Kℓ⁡(𝐳5​j,𝐳j⋆)],\min_{\mathcal{C}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D},\,\boldsymbol{\theta}\sim p(\boldsymbol{\theta})}\Big[\sum_{j=1}^{K}\ell\left(\mathbf{z}_{5j},\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{j}\right)\Big], (1)

where 𝒟\mathcal{D} denotes the demonstrations and ℓ\ell is the discrepancy between 𝐳5​j\mathbf{z}_{5j} and 𝐳j⋆\mathbf{z}^{\star}_{j} in position, heading and speed. Eq. (1) addresses control rather than prediction: the control inputs are the unknowns, and the model maps them to the states that the demonstrations record. The planning decoder is trained jointly with its own loss.

III-B Control Decoder

The learned planner regenerates its reference at every perception update, conditioned on the current vehicle state and reliable only within the preview horizon. A controller that relies solely on this reference inherits its uncertainty. To mitigate this limitation, the control decoder receives not only the explicit reference but also the raw scene tokens and the planner’s intermediate features, enabling compensation for planning inaccuracies through richer contextual information.

III-B1 Memory Tokens

The perception backbone and the planning decoder follow TF++ [30]. The fused bird’s-eye-view feature is projected and positionally encoded into perception tokens 𝐌\mathbf{M}, augmented by a speed and navigation token. A transformer with learned queries 𝐐p\mathbf{Q}_{p} attends to 𝐌\mathbf{M} and produces planning tokens 𝐏\mathbf{P}, from which a GRU decodes the route ℛ\mathcal{R} and a softmax head outputs the speed distribution 𝐩v\mathbf{p}^{v}.

The control decoder is an independent three-layer transformer whose memory

𝐒=[\displaystyle\mathbf{S}=\big[ ϕM​(𝐌);ϕP​(𝐏);ER​(ℛref);\displaystyle\phi_{M}(\mathbf{M});\phi_{P}(\mathbf{P});E_{R}(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}); (2)
Ev(𝐩vref);Eo(𝐨);Ed(𝐝)]\displaystyle E_{v}(\mathbf{p}^{v}_{\mathrm{ref}});E_{o}(\mathbf{o});E_{d}(\mathbf{d})\big]

concatenates four groups of tokens, formed by learned adapters ϕM\phi_{M}, ϕP\phi_{P} and learned embeddings ERE_{R}, EvE_{v}, EoE_{o}, EdE_{d}. The feature interface ϕM​(𝐌)\phi_{M}(\mathbf{M}), ϕP​(𝐏)\phi_{P}(\mathbf{P}) lets the controller attend to the scene and the planner’s intermediate representation. The explicit reference, per-point route tokens ER​(ℛref)E_{R}(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}}) and a speed token Ev​(𝐩refv)E_{v}(\mathbf{p}^{v}_{\mathrm{ref}}), keeps the interpretable interface of the planner. The state-feedback token Eo​(𝐨)E_{o}(\mathbf{o}), with 𝐨=[vx,ravg]⊤\mathbf{o}=[v_{x},r_{\mathrm{avg}}]^{\top}, closes the loop on speed and yaw rate and deliberately excludes accelerations. The disturbance-estimate token Ed​(𝐝)E_{d}(\mathbf{d}) carries the observer estimates. Here ravgr_{\mathrm{avg}} is the yaw rate averaged over one label period TlabT_{\mathrm{lab}}. At deployment, the reference (ℛref,𝐩refv)(\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{ref}},\mathbf{p}^{v}_{\mathrm{ref}}) is the planner output (ℛ,𝐩v)(\mathcal{R},\mathbf{p}^{v}). In training, it is replaced by the ground truth with probability 0.5, and the feature tokens are masked with probability 0.1, so that the controller can also operate on the explicit reference alone.

III-B2 Rate-Consistent Control-Input Knots

The decoder output yields the knots

𝐔=tanh⁡(MLP⁡(Decc⁡(𝐐c,𝐒)))∈[−1,1](K+1)×2,\mathbf{U}=\tanh\left(\operatorname{MLP}\left(\operatorname{Dec}_{c}\left(\mathbf{Q}_{c},\mathbf{S}\right)\right)\right)\in[-1,1]^{(K+1)\times 2}, (3)

where Decc\operatorname{Dec}_{c} denotes this transformer with K+1K+1 learned queries 𝐐c\mathbf{Q}_{c}. Each knot 𝐮j=[ux,j,us,j]⊤\mathbf{u}_{j}=[u_{x,j},u_{s,j}]^{\top} is converted to vehicle commands by 𝐜⁡(𝐮)=[[ux]+,[−ux]+,us]⊤\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{u})=\left[[u_{x}]_{+},[-u_{x}]_{+},u_{s}\right]^{\top}, where [x]+=max⁡{x,0}[x]_{+}=\max\{x,0\}. The single signed longitudinal input uxu_{x} excludes simultaneous throttle and brake and keeps the longitudinal acceleration monotone in uxu_{x}. As absolute commands are bounded by tanh\tanh, the knots require no previous-command input and cannot drift like an integrator.

Parameterizing the control inputs at the control rate would introduce far more free inputs per sample than the state labels can constrain, overfitting to the temporal aliasing. DIVA therefore places the knot values at the label rate, but integrates the model and executes the commands at the control rate. The knots are interpolated to the control period by FOH,

𝐮¯k=(1−{k5})​𝐮⌊k/5⌋+{k5}​𝐮⌊k/5⌋+1,\bar{\mathbf{u}}_{k}=\left(1-\left\{\tfrac{k}{5}\right\}\right)\mathbf{u}_{\lfloor k/5\rfloor}+\left\{\tfrac{k}{5}\right\}\mathbf{u}_{\lfloor k/5\rfloor+1}, (4)

for k=0,…,H−1k=0,\ldots,H-1, where ⌊⋅⌋\lfloor\cdot\rfloor and {⋅}\{\cdot\} denote the integer and fractional parts. The loss is evaluated only at the control steps that coincide with the label instants, with control step 0 applying knot 0 exactly. Retaining the full control-rate integration is essential: coarsening the model to one step per knot would introduce numerical distortion, and the controller would learn to compensate for this model bias rather than for the true vehicle dynamics. During deployment, the control decoder executes at every control step with the latest state feedback 𝐨\mathbf{o} and disturbance estimate 𝐝\mathbf{d}, applying only knot 0 in a receding-horizon fashion. The knot parameterization therefore serves purely as a training-time mechanism for temporal credit assignment and does not reduce the closed-loop control rate.

III-C Identified Differentiable Vehicle Dynamics

The vehicle dynamics model ℱ\mathcal{F} constitutes the sole differentiable path from the control decoder’s output knots to the predicted vehicle states; consequently, the controller implicitly adapts its commands to the characteristics of this model. This coupling imposes three requirements on ℱ\mathcal{F}. First, the model must faithfully capture the actuator dynamics that govern the vehicle’s response to a given command. Second, it must provide well-defined gradients throughout the controller’s operating envelope, including at standstill. Third, it must generalize beyond the identification excitations and remain accurate under the command distribution induced by the trained controller. In addition, ℱ\mathcal{F} serves a fourth role by parameterizing the vehicle-side model mismatch for online estimation.

III-C1 Model Structure

The state of the model is

𝐳=[X,Y,ψ,vx,vy,r,c~s,c~t,c~b,ad,ab,χ]⊤,\mathbf{z}=\left[X,Y,\psi,v_{x},v_{y},r,\tilde{c}_{s},\tilde{c}_{t},\tilde{c}_{b},a_{d},a_{b},\chi\right]^{\top}, (5)

which comprises the vehicle pose (X,Y,ψ)(X,Y,\psi), the longitudinal and lateral velocities vxv_{x} and vyv_{y}, the yaw rate rr, and the actuator states: the rate-limited steering, throttle and brake inputs c~s\tilde{c}_{s}, c~t\tilde{c}_{t} and c~b\tilde{c}_{b}, the lagged powertrain and brake accelerations ada_{d} and aba_{b}, and a wheel-lock indicator χ∈{0,1}\chi\in\{0,1\}.

The model explicitly represents the actuator chain from commanded input to vehicle response. Each command first passes through the vehicle’s slew-rate limiter, which enforces the physical rate constraints on steering, throttle and brake. The powertrain acceleration ada_{d} is governed by a static map 𝒜⁡(vx,c~t)\mathcal{A}(v_{x},\tilde{c}_{t}), filtered through a first-order lag; this map encodes the steady-state acceleration on a flat road, accounting for road load, engine braking and the gear selected by the transmission shift schedule at the current speed. The brake acceleration aba_{b} is similarly modeled as a constant deceleration abrk<0a_{\mathrm{brk}}<0:

ax,k=ad,k+1+ab,k+1−gsinγk,a_{x,k}=a_{d,k+1}+a_{b,k+1}-g\sin\gamma_{k}, (6)

where gg is the gravitational acceleration and γk\gamma_{k} is the road grade angle, positive uphill. Two discrete regimes, a wheel lock in the first gear and a standstill hold under braking, complete the longitudinal channel. In the lateral channel, the steering input sets the road-wheel angle through a speed-dependent steering limit and the Ackermann geometry. A single-track model with saturating lateral tire forces yields vyv_{y} and rr, and blends into the kinematic single-track model at low speed.

The model advances by one control period TsT_{s} per step and is formulated directly in discrete time rather than as a numerical discretization of continuous-time dynamics; empirically, reducing the integration step below TsT_{s} yields no improvement in open-loop accuracy on held-out drives (Fig. 2(f)). This discrete-time formulation also motivates the design choice: the control-input knots are interpolated to the control rate and integrated at that rate, rather than integrated at the coarser label rate. The model parameters are identified through a three-tier procedure in which each tier is fitted with all preceding tiers held fixed: specification-level parameters are drawn from the vehicle datasheet, calibration-level parameters are obtained from constant-input, step and coast-down experiments, and the remaining parameters are identified from step-steer and swept-sine maneuvers. Appendix -A provides the complete model equations, the identification protocol, the resulting parameter values, and a validation against measured vehicle data.

III-C2 Gradients Through Non-Smooth Actuator Characteristics

Several elements of ℱ\mathcal{F} are non-smooth: the split of uxu_{x} into throttle and brake, the floor [⋅]+[\cdot]_{+} on the speed, the dead band of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the discrete regimes, the slew-rate limiter and the clipping of the commands. A zero gradient there would stop learning exactly where the vehicle launches and stops. The split and the floor therefore use a leaky straight-through estimator [32]: the forward pass computes [x]+[x]_{+}, and the backward pass uses the slope 1 for x>0x>0 and ϵst=0.1\epsilon_{\mathrm{st}}=0.1 otherwise. Gradients thus still flow at standstill and in the dead band. The indicators of the discrete regimes are detached in the backward pass, and the limiter and the clipping keep the subgradient. The Ackermann relation is implemented in a form that is continuously differentiable at zero steering (Appendix -A). A finite-difference check confirms the analytical gradients with respect to the knots.

III-C3 Policy-Induced Model Shift and On-Policy Re-Identification

System identification relies on designed excitations, such as constant inputs, steps and bang-bang sequences, which hold a few discrete input levels (Fig. 2(a)). A controller trained through the model instead applies smooth, moderate throttle and modulated braking. It drives the model into regimes that the identification data cover only sparsely, and inherits the model error there. This paper terms the effect policy-induced model shift, the model-side counterpart of the covariate shift of imitation learning; it instantiates identification for control, under which the identification experiment should reflect the operating conditions of the controller [33].

Replaying open loop the closed-loop telemetry of a first controller trained through the calibrated model reveals a systematic speed over-prediction (Fig. 2(e)). The error stems from the upshift torque interruptions, the shift points and the brake-release lag (Fig. 2(b)–(d)). The correction has deliberately low capacity with 12 scalars in total: it edits only the tractive part of 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the two lag constants (Appendix -A). It largely eliminates the speed bias under the first controller’s commands and improves the accuracy on the held-out drives (Fig. 2(e) and (f)). DIVA is trained through the re-identified model.

III-C4 Mismatch Parameterization

The deployed vehicle never matches the training model exactly: the model structure is simplified, and the mass, actuator gains, biases and friction change in operation. These deviations are parameterized by

𝜽=[ks,bs,bt,kd,kb,km,kμ,dx]⊤.\boldsymbol{\theta}=\left[k_{s},b_{s},b_{t},k_{d},k_{b},k_{m},k_{\mu},d_{x}\right]^{\top}. (7)

The steering gain ksk_{s}, the steering bias bsb_{s} and the throttle bias btb_{t} act on the commands before the slew-rate limiter, cs←ks​cs+bsc_{s}\leftarrow k_{s}c_{s}+b_{s} and ct←ct+btc_{t}\leftarrow c_{t}+b_{t}. The powertrain and brake gains kdk_{d} and kbk_{b} scale ada_{d} and aba_{b}. The mass factor kmk_{m} divides the longitudinal acceleration and scales the mass, the yaw moment of inertia and the cornering stiffnesses jointly, which leaves the lateral response unchanged. The tire–road friction factor kμk_{\mu} scales the tire saturation and the locked-wheel deceleration, and dxd_{x} adds a longitudinal acceleration disturbance. The acceleration in Eq. (6) thus becomes ax,k=(kdad,k+1+kbab,k+1)/km+dx−gsinγka_{x,k}=(k_{d}a_{d,k+1}+k_{b}a_{b,k+1})/k_{m}+d_{x}-g\sin\gamma_{k}, and the nominal value 𝜽0=[1,0,0,1,1,1,1,0]⊤\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0}=[1,0,0,1,1,1,1,0]^{\top} recovers the identified model.

Given that only speed and yaw rate are available as measurements, the individual components of 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta} acting on the same dynamic channel are not separately observable. The observable quantities reduce to two lumped deviations,

b¯s\displaystyle\bar{b}_{s} =bs+(ks−1)​cs,\displaystyle=b_{s}+\left(k_{s}-1\right)c_{s}, (8)
d¯x\displaystyle\bar{d}_{x} =dx+(kdkm−1)​ad+(kbkm−1)​ab−g​sin⁡γ,\displaystyle=d_{x}+\left(\frac{k_{d}}{k_{m}}-1\right)a_{d}+\left(\frac{k_{b}}{k_{m}}-1\right)a_{b}-g\sin\gamma,

representing the net steering bias and the total unexplained longitudinal acceleration. These two lumped deviations constitute the disturbance signals on which the control decoder is conditioned: during training they are computed analytically from 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}, while at deployment they are estimated online. The identified model consequently fulfills three roles: it serves as the differentiable plant for controller training, as the process model of the online observer, and, through the observer’s estimates, as the dynamics model underlying the classical baseline controllers.

III-D Dynamics-in-the-Loop Imitation Learning

With the differentiable chain from control decoder to vehicle states now defined, this section addresses the training procedure: the supervision signal and loss formulation, the strategies that ensure closed-loop validity and robustness to model mismatch, and the joint training of the controller with the planner.

III-D1 State-Space Supervision With Identifiability-Aware Control-Input Anchor

The design of the supervision signal is governed by two properties of the expert demonstrations. First, the expert commands are recorded at a rate lower than the control rate, so the raw control-input labels suffer from temporal aliasing and cannot faithfully reproduce the expert motion; in contrast, control-input knots recovered from the expert states via gradient-based inversion yield substantially more accurate trajectories. Second, the longitudinal command is not identifiable from the vehicle motion at standstill, since any command within the pedal dead band produces zero acceleration and leaves the vehicle state unchanged.

The supervision therefore combines a state-space loss with a control-input anchor, where the anchor is weighted more heavily in regimes where the state provides insufficient gradient signal (e.g., standstill) or where the control-input labels are reliable. Specifically, the state loss projects the position error of the roll-out at each label instant jj onto the expert heading direction, decomposing it into a longitudinal component ex,je_{x,j} and a lateral component ey,je_{y,j}, alongside the heading error eψ,je_{\psi,j} and the speed error ev,je_{v,j}, all defined as the difference between rollouts and demonstration:

ℒstate=⟨\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{state}}=\Big\langle wy​Hub0.1⁡(ey,j)+wx​ℓκ​(ex,j)\displaystyle w_{y}\operatorname{Hub}_{0.1}(e_{y,j})+w_{x}\,\ell_{\kappa}(e_{x,j}) (9)
+wψHub0.02(eψ,j)+wvℓκ(ev,j)⟩ω+wRℒR,\displaystyle+w_{\psi}\operatorname{Hub}_{0.02}(e_{\psi,j})+w_{v}\,\ell_{\kappa}(e_{v,j})\Big\rangle_{\omega}+w_{R}\mathcal{L}_{R},

where Hubς\operatorname{Hub}_{\varsigma} is the Huber function with transition point ς\varsigma, ℓκ\ell_{\kappa} is the risk-sensitive loss in Eq. (11), ⟨⋅⟩ω\langle\cdot\rangle_{\omega} is the mean over samples and valid label instants weighted by the sample weight ω\omega, and ℒR\mathcal{L}_{R} ties each rolled-out position to the lane center via the route label. The sample weight emphasizes decision-informative rare samples: launch and stop windows, onsets of emergency braking, and hard-steering samples. The control-input anchor

ℒanc=∑jΩj​[ηj​Hub0.2⁡(ux,j−ux,j⋆)+4​|us,j−us,j⋆|]∑jΩj\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anc}}=\frac{\sum_{j}\Omega_{j}\left[\eta_{j}\operatorname{Hub}_{0.2}\left(u_{x,j}-u^{\star}_{x,j}\right)+4\left|u_{s,j}-u^{\star}_{s,j}\right|\right]}{\sum_{j}\Omega_{j}} (10)

encodes identifiability: the longitudinal weight ηj\eta_{j} is strong where the state loss is blind (standstill braking or launch), weak while moving (aliased labels), raised on sustained emergency brakes (clean labels), and zero on recovery samples. The weight Ωj\Omega_{j} combines the sample weight ω\omega with a decay along the horizon and a raise at standstill. The steering term is L1, robust to aliased steering peaks, and scaled for its smaller range. With weights wΔw_{\Delta}, wJw_{J}, wayw_{a_{y}} and wζw_{\zeta}, a regularizer ℒreg\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}} penalizes knot-to-knot changes, longitudinal jerk, lateral acceleration aya_{y} beyond a comfort limit, and tire utilization ζ=maxi⁡|Fy,i|/(μi​Fz,i)\zeta=\max_{i}|F_{y,i}|/(\mu_{i}F_{z,i}) of Eq. (16) beyond a limit.

III-D2 Closing the Loop

Four mechanisms narrow the open-loop-to-closed-loop transfer gap:

  • •

    Risk-sensitive loss. In braking situations the distribution of future trajectories is bimodal (the vehicle either stops or proceeds), and a symmetric loss converges to the conditional median between the two modes, resulting in braking commands that are delayed. DIVA instead applies an asymmetric quantile loss

    ℓκ(e)=(1+κι𝕀[e>0])|e|,\ell_{\kappa}(e)=\left(1+\kappa\,\iota\,\mathbb{I}[e>0]\right)|e|, (11)

    to the longitudinal and speed errors ex,je_{x,j} and ev,je_{v,j}, which are positive when the roll-out is ahead of or faster than the expert. The indicator ι∈{0,1}\iota\in\{0,1\} activates the asymmetry (κ=3\kappa=3) in braking situations; the minimizer is then the 1/(2+κ)1/(2+\kappa) quantile, so the roll-out commits to stopping once the stop-class probability exceeds 1/(2+κ)=0.21/(2+\kappa)=0.2. A braking situation is flagged when the vehicle is moving and either (i) a hazard has been flagged or braked for within the horizon while the speed reference signals a stop, or (ii) an emergency brake has occurred within 0.5 s. An auxiliary head predicts the emergency-braking flags with a binary cross-entropy loss ℒhaz\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{haz}}.

  • •

    Causal state feedback. Including acceleration states in the feedback token introduces a causal shortcut [34], since these states effectively encode the previous command and allow the network to copy rather than predict it. This shortcut manifests after each upshift torque interruption, where the closed loop settles into a self-confirming low-acceleration equilibrium. The state-feedback token is therefore restricted to vxv_{x} and ravgr_{\mathrm{avg}}, where the yaw rate is computed via a backward finite difference to preserve strict causality; a central difference would implicitly leak the next expert state into the current observation.

  • •

    Recovery samples. With probability 0.3, the initial speed of both the roll-out and 𝐨\mathbf{o} is perturbed while the targets remain the expert states, so that the controller learns speed feedback from off-trajectory states without additional sensor data.

  • •

    Beyond-preview reference distrust. With probability 0.5, the reference route beyond the preview distance is shifted along its normal by an offset that grows quadratically from zero at the preview boundary to a random value at the final point, so that the controller learns to rely on its own scene understanding.

III-D3 Training Under Model Mismatch

In training, p⁡(𝜽)p(\boldsymbol{\theta}) places probability 0.5 on the nominal value 𝜽0\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0} and spreads the rest over randomized deviations. The targets remain the nominal expert states, so the controller learns commands that reproduce the expert behavior under mismatch. The controller is informed of the mismatch through the same lumped deviations the observer would report:

𝐝=ν​[b¯s+ns,d¯x+nx, 1]⊤,ν∼Bernoulli⁡(0.7),\mathbf{d}=\nu\left[\bar{b}_{s}+n_{s},\;\bar{d}_{x}+n_{x},\;1\right]^{\top},\qquad\nu\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.7), (12)

where b¯s\bar{b}_{s} and d¯x\bar{d}_{x} are the lumped deviations in Eq. (8), evaluated once at the steady state of the expert command at tt and held over the horizon, nsn_{s} and nxn_{x} are zero-mean Gaussian noises emulating the estimation error, the last component flags an available estimate, and withholding the estimate (ν=0\nu=0) keeps the controller valid before observer convergence.

III-D4 Gradient Gate for Joint Training

The planner and the control decoder are trained jointly from scratch on the frozen pretrained backbone, and the control loss reaches the planner through the feature interface and the explicit reference in Eq. (2). On the shared layers, the control-loss gradient is negligible at initialization but grows to dominate the planning-loss gradient at convergence. Every tensor that the control branch receives from the planner therefore passes a gate

𝒢λ​(𝐱)=sg⁡(𝐱)+λ⁡(𝐱−sg⁡(𝐱)),\mathcal{G}_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x})=\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{x})+\lambda\left(\mathbf{x}-\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{x})\right), (13)

where sg\operatorname{sg} is the stop-gradient operator. The gate is the identity in the forward pass and scales the backward pass by a constant λ=0.1\lambda=0.1, which brings the two gradients to the same order at convergence. Unlike a loss weight, it leaves every forward value and the planner’s own gradient untouched; λ=0\lambda=0 reproduces the training signal of a standalone planner exactly. The complete objective is

ℒ=ℒstate+wa​ℒanc+ℒreg+wh​ℒhaz+wp​ℒplan,\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{state}}+w_{a}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{anc}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}+w_{h}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{haz}}+w_{p}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}}, (14)

where ℒplan\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{plan}} is the route and speed loss of the planning decoder [30].

III-E Asynchronous Execution and Online Disturbance Estimation

During training, the controller is evaluated on open-loop roll-outs initialized from recorded states, with perception available at every step. At deployment, however, two additional challenges arise: the control decoder must execute at every control step while perception updates arrive at a lower rate, and the deployed vehicle inevitably deviates from the nominal dynamics model.

III-E1 Asynchronous Execution

Because perception cannot run at the control rate, the tokens in Eq. (2) are split into two groups by update rate. The tokens derived from perception, ϕM​(𝐌)\phi_{M}(\mathbf{M}), ϕP​(𝐏)\phi_{P}(\mathbf{P}) and the speed token, are cached at fpercf_{\mathrm{perc}} together with the route and the pose of their sensor frame, while Eo​(𝐨)E_{o}(\mathbf{o}), Ed​(𝐝)E_{d}(\mathbf{d}) and the route tokens of the vehicle-relative route are recomputed at every control step. Between perception updates, the cached route is transformed to the current pose by a rigid-body transform,

𝝆i′=[cos⁡Δ​ψsin⁡Δ​ψ−sin⁡Δ​ψcos⁡Δ​ψ]⁡(𝝆i−[Δ​XΔ​Y]),\boldsymbol{\rho}^{\prime}_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\Delta\psi&\sin\Delta\psi\\ -\sin\Delta\psi&\cos\Delta\psi\end{bmatrix}\left(\boldsymbol{\rho}_{i}-\begin{bmatrix}\Delta X\\ \Delta Y\end{bmatrix}\right), (15)

where (Δ​X,Δ​Y,Δ​ψ)(\Delta X,\Delta Y,\Delta\psi) denotes the displacement of the vehicle relative to the sensor frame of the cached route. After arc-length resampling of the transformed route, only the three-layer control decoder needs to be evaluated, constituting the fast path of the system. To inform the control decoder of the staleness of its cached perception, a latency embedding encodes both the elapsed time since the last perception update and the accumulated ego-motion (Δ​X,Δ​Y,Δ​ψ)(\Delta X,\Delta Y,\Delta\psi) over that interval. This embedding is initialized to zero, so that the decoder’s behavior is unaffected when perception is synchronous with control. During training, latency robustness is encouraged by randomly delaying the perception inputs by one or two label periods with probability 0.3. In the limiting case where perception runs at every control step with zero latency, the asynchronous execution path degenerates to standard synchronous operation.

III-E2 Online Disturbance Observer

The lumped deviations defined in Eq. (8) are estimated online by an augmented unscented Kalman filter (UKF). The filter state is [vx,vy,r,bs,dx]⊤[v_{x},v_{y},r,b_{s},d_{x}]^{\top}, with speed and yaw rate serving as measurements. The process model consists of one control step of ℱ\mathcal{F} evaluated at the nominal parameters 𝜽0\boldsymbol{\theta}_{0}, in which b¯s\bar{b}_{s} and d¯x\bar{d}_{x} are augmented as random-walk states; the filter estimates of these augmented states thus converge to b¯s\bar{b}_{s} and d¯x\bar{d}_{x}. The road grade γ\gamma is set to zero in the process model so that its effect is absorbed into the longitudinal deviation dxd_{x}. To prevent uninformative measurements from degrading the estimates, each deviation is frozen in operating regimes where the corresponding measurement channel carries negligible observability, such as low-speed steering for b¯s\bar{b}_{s} or near-standstill braking for d¯x\bar{d}_{x}. Additionally, a speed innovation exceeding TsT_{s} times the maximum tire-limited acceleration triggers a temporary freeze of both estimates, safeguarding the filter against corruption from collision events. The resulting estimates b^s\hat{b}_{s} and d^x\hat{d}_{x} are assembled into the disturbance token 𝐝=[b^s,d^x,1]⊤\mathbf{d}=[\hat{b}_{s},\hat{d}_{x},1]^{\top} that the control decoder receives as input. Two quantities are deliberately excluded from the estimation: tire-road friction, which is observable from speed and yaw rate only during the brief transients in which the tires saturate and is therefore not reliably estimable in steady driving, and the brake gain deviation, which is not separately identifiable and enters the filter through d¯x\bar{d}_{x}.

IV Experiments

The experiments address four questions: (1) does extending the differentiable chain to vehicle control improve closed-loop driving and execution quality? (2) which components of DIVA account for the effect? (3) how does the model behave under sustained vehicle dynamics mismatch, compared with classical controllers that use the same identified model and observer? (4) what does the control loop cost, and does it remain effective when perception runs slower than the control rate? Section IV-F presents case studies.

IV-A Experimental Setup and Baselines

IV-A1 Benchmark and Training Data

All closed-loop experiments use the Bench2Drive-220 benchmark [35] with its official metrics: driving score (DS), success rate (SR), efficiency, comfortness and five ability scores. Training follows [30] on the PDM-Lite dataset [36], recorded at 4 Hz, with the same route filter and data split; the perception backbone is pretrained as in [30] and frozen.

IV-A2 Evaluation Subsets

The ablation, mismatch and perception-rate studies use Hard-52, a subset of 52 routes from Bench2Drive-220 that emphasize lateral and longitudinal control complexity: 23 lateral maneuvers, 13 junction turns, 12 merging or highway routes and 4 emergency-braking routes, fixed before any ablation run. On the remaining routes, DIVA and DIVA+PID are nearly tied (92.14 vs. 91.20 DS). The model mismatch study additionally uses a traffic-free maneuver suite of 16 routes grouped into six families (junction turns, highway, lane changes, stop-and-go, emergency braking, curves). Background traffic and scenario actors are removed except in the emergency-braking family; the evaluation is then nearly deterministic, so tracking metrics resolve the controllers and a single trial per condition suffices.

IV-A3 Shared Stack and Controllers

All configurations share the same backbone, rules and safety logic of [30]; only the planner and the controller change. Two planners are used: the baseline planner (trained alone) and the joint planner (trained together with the control decoder of DIVA). The compared configurations are:

  • •

    TF++ [30]: the baseline planner with its PID, the most widely used controller of closed-loop driving in Bench2Drive: a lateral PID towards a look-ahead point and a longitudinal PID with full-brake and saturating-throttle branches.

  • •

    MPC+DOB: the baseline planner with an MPC that shares the identified model, the disturbance observer (DOB) of Section
